IRAQ WAR & DIGITAL PRIVACY

CLASS PROJECT

About this class project

This website looks at what happened to privacy during the Iraq War era, from government access to phone records to the collection of fingerprints and iris scans.

AI-ASSISTED DRAFT · REAL RATING PENDING REVIEW

Who this is for

Jordan is the audience persona for this project. She's a college student who uses Instagram, Snapchat, Google, and AI chatbots every day. She knows these services collect information and likes how convenient they are. She hasn't spent much time looking into the history of privacy.

Working user-need statement

Jordan needs a short explanation, backed by sources, of how surveillance grew during the Iraq War era. That history can help her understand the privacy questions behind technology she already uses.

The timeline keeps the dates straight, and the short sections explain each law or program on its own. References to everyday apps give readers a familiar starting point. Using an app still involves very different choices and pressures from living under military occupation.

Connection to the course

In Data Feminism, D’Ignazio and Klein argue that understanding data means understanding where it comes from. This site follows that idea by asking who collected the information, what gave them the authority to do it, and what could happen to the person in the record (D’Ignazio & Klein, 2020, Chapter 6).

Their idea of making labor visible also matters here. The AI disclosure below explains how this draft was made and what work remains (D’Ignazio & Klein, 2020, Chapter 7).

How the sources are used

The 2001 PATRIOT Act is one of the project's primary sources. Its date is important: it passed before the 2003 invasion. Keeping those dates visible helps explain where the Iraq War fits into the wider War on Terror (Office of the Historian, n.d.; USA PATRIOT Act, 2001).

The 2014 oversight report on Section 215, the 2008 FISA Amendments Act, and the 2015 USA FREEDOM Act help explain what the government could collect and how those powers changed. The summaries keep phone metadata separate from the contents of conversations. They describe the law during this period, rather than today's rules (FISA Amendments Act, 2008, § 101; Office of the Director of National Intelligence, 2015, p. 1; Privacy and Civil Liberties Oversight Board [PCLOB], 2014a, p. 114; PCLOB, 2014b, pp. 21–22; USA FREEDOM Act, 2015, §§ 101, 103, 109).

The GAO report describes the military's use of biometrics. Stefka Hristova’s peer-reviewed article looks at how those systems helped classify people as security threats in Iraq. This site focuses on one part of her argument: confirming someone's identity and judging that person are different decisions (Hristova, 2014, pp. 516–517; U.S. Government Accountability Office [GAO], 2008b, p. 7).

Most of these sources come from U.S. institutions or academic researchers. They can't tell the whole story of how Iraqis experienced surveillance. Where a government report covers Iraq and Afghanistan together, the site makes that clear.

How AI was used

Generative AI helped find research leads, summarize sources, draft the text, and build the layout, code, and illustration. The student provided the topic, assignment, audience persona, and feedback that changed the site's direction. AI contributed substantially to this draft.

Source details and key claims were checked against government and publisher pages during drafting. The student still needs to read the sources, make their own revisions, and keep a record of their work.

  • REAL rating: still needs the course's definitions and the author's final review.
  • Work log: the assignment requires at least three hours of project work and a moderate level of human involvement. This draft doesn't claim that work is finished.
  • Academic source: check that Hristova’s article isn't a required class reading.
  • Safety charter: check the final piece against the team's actual charter before saying it meets those commitments.

Checking the sources

The source check on November 19, 2026 used government publication records, the original reports and laws, and the journal's article PDF and issue contents. The citations use APA 7 author–date format, with page or section numbers to help you find the passage. That check corrected the GAO-08-1065 date to September 26, 2008 and clarified that the Section 215 finding came from a 3–2 board majority (PCLOB, 2014b, p. 16; GAO, 2008b).

The site keeps the dates in order and makes clear which claims come from government reports and which are a scholar's interpretation. A biometric match doesn't prove guilt. There are no invented Iraqi accounts, audience responses, or work hours, and the graphics don't use anyone's personal or biometric records.

Privacy on this website

This site doesn’t save or send your choices in the interactive sections. The phone records in the opening example are made up, and the site loads no external video player. Source links take you to other websites with their own privacy practices.
